transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-14
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Evan Mitchell (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (Midland Head of ML), Marcus Flynn (Midland Infra Lead), Jasmine Wu (Midland Product)

Summary:
Short call to understand Midland's model selection constraints: they are evaluating open models for a customer-facing analytics assistant. Primary concerns: context length (long documents and multi-doc reasoning), multilingual support (esp. Spanish & Mandarin), and reliable tool-calling for data retrieval and internal APIs. They want to understand Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs and to run a short benchmark/pilot.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and infra constraints
- Typical prompt/document sizes and required context window
- Multilingual coverage and hallucination risks
- Tool-calling patterns (retrieval, db lookups, external APIs)
- Security/compliance (SOC2, SSO/SAML, VPC)
- Pricing/latency tradeoffs and pilot logistics

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Evan, account lead for Redwood. Quick role call?
[00:06] Lena: Hi, Lena here, head of ML at Midland.
[00:08] Marcus: Marcus, infra lead.
[00:10] Jasmine: Jasmine, product.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, SE on the inference side — I'll handle the technical bits.

[01:00] Evan: Great. We got your note about needing long context and multi-lingual support. Can you walk through the typical user flow — what are the inputs and how many docs or tokens are we hitting?
[01:15] Lena: Sure. Our assistant needs to answer customer queries about large enterprise invoices, contracts, and support tickets. Typical session will include a user question plus piping in 3–8 related docs. Document sizes range, sometimes a 200-page contract, but generally we chunk into 5–15k token passages. End-to-end context can be 50–150k tokens if we naively concatenate.
[01:42] Priya: OK so you often need effectively a 64k+ window or you rely on retrieval to narrow down context?
[01:50] Lena: We prefer retrieval but want the model to keep a fairly large window for cross-document reasoning. We've tried a cheap roll-your-own approach with local reranker + 8k model and it breaks on complex edge cases.
[02:10] Marcus: Also latency matters — customers expect answers under 2s for short queries, 5–6s for longer combo queries.

[03:05] Priya: That helps. For context length we typically recommend combining a retrieval front-end with Redwood's KV prefix caching and the runtime's support for long-context models (we can run 32k/65k variants depending on model). There's tradeoffs in cost and latency.
[03:25] Marcus: Curious about which open models we should try — we've heard about LlamaX-70B, Falcon-40B, and some of the newer grouped models. Also what about quantized variants?
[03:40] Priya: Right. In our experience: Falcon-style models are good for shorter contexts and are cost-efficient; Llama-family larger contexts are better for nuanced reasoning; some community 65k-tokens forks exist but you lose some safety evals. We can run comparisons. Quantization (4-bit/qlora-ish) reduces cost but can slightly change behavior — Redwood Optimize can recommend quant/throughput profiles per workload.

[04:55] Jasmine: How does tool-calling fit here? We need the assistant to call internal APIs to fetch up-to-date invoice status, and call a vector DB for retrieval. Need deterministic behavior: e.g., if the tool says invoice is unpaid, model shouldn't hallucinate.
[05:10] Priya: We support structured tool-calling via our function-calling interface — you can register function signatures, we do deterministic routing to functions and provide a fallback if the model returns something unexpected. For strict determinism, we recommend orchestration where the model suggests which function and the Redwood runtime executes it and returns the raw result to the model for final phrasing.
[05:45] Lena: Good. We also have multilingual needs: Spanish and Simplified Chinese primarily. How robust are the open models there?
[05:55] Priya: Several high-tier open models have strong Spanish coverage; Chinese is variable — some community models do well but require evaluation. We recommend targeted eval sets per language (we can help craft those) and measuring hallucination and factuality.

[07:10] Evan: On deployment — you mentioned compliance concerns. Marcus, can you walk us through where you'd prefer Redwood to run? Hosted, Dedicated, Private?
[07:19] Marcus: For POC we can start with hosted to iterate quickly. Long term we expect either Dedicated reserved capacity (if cost/latency preferable) or Private in our VPC for data residency and strict network control. We need SSO/SAML and audit logs at minimum; SOC2 compliance would be ideal.
[07:41] Priya: Those are common. Hosted gives fastest time to value; Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools with predictable throughput; Private (VPC/private control plane or on-prem) gives you the highest network isolation and KMS/HSM integrations.

[08:30] Jasmine: How does the routing/fallback work if the dedicated pool is saturated? We have spikes end of month.
[08:38] Priya: Redwood can route by policy: fall back to a compatible hosted model variant or a lower-cost model in a different pool. You can set SLOs so high-priority routes always get capacity. For billing, you'd only pay for what you route to.

[09:10] Marcus: Can we pin a model for compliance reasons? Like, pin LlamaX-70b-32k?
[09:16] Priya: Yes — model version pinning and rollouts are supported. Also can run canary deploys and A/B tests using the console.

[10:00] Evan: Let's talk numbers briefly — rough latency and cost expectations for a 32k vs 65k context on hosted vs dedicated?
[10:12] Priya: High-level: 32k on a high-memory GPU with optimized kernels — for a 70B model you might see 2–5s depending on token output. 65k will typically add 30–80% latency overhead depending on batch size and KV cache usage. Cost is model and infra dependent; dedicated can be significantly cheaper per-token at scale due to reserved pricing and tuned kernels. We'll send a price matrix.

[11:05] Lena: On hallucinations — we need to track regressions. Does Redwood do evals and alerts for quality drift?
[11:13] Priya: Yes — Redwood Optimize and Console can run prompt sets, detect regressions, and tie them to model/version changes. We can run automatic regression alerts on your evaluation prompts.

[12:20] Jasmine: For the demo/pilot, we'd want to: 1) validate 65k retrieval+reasoning on a sample doc set, 2) test tool-calling determinism with our invoice API, 3) compare Spanish/Chinese response quality.
[12:35] Evan: That maps to a 1-week technical pilot: Redwood SE runs bench with your documents + seeds and we run hosted + dedicated comparisons. Marcus, you'll need to give network access or a small staging dataset.
[12:47] Marcus: We'll provide sanitized data and an API endpoint in a staging VPC. For hosted tests we can expose a temporary proxy. For dedicated pilot — how long can we run reserved capacity?
[12:58] Priya: For pilots we usually spin up short-term dedicated pools (week-long) or use burst on hosted. We'll include options in the pilot proposal.

[14:05] Lena: What's the typical timeline for a security review? We need SOC2 docs, encryption attestations, and a pen-test report.
[14:12] Evan: We can share the SOC2 Type II report and an architecture brief. Security review usually 1–2 weeks depending on your infosec cadence. For Private/VPC deployments, we can show KMS/HSM integration notes and audit log samples.

[15:30] Marcus: Any differences in log retention when on private? We can't allow long-term retention of PII.
[15:36] Priya: Private gives you more control. You can configure retention and opt-out of certain telemetry. For hosted, we have configurable retention windows and options to disable storing request payloads if needed. We'll include specifics in the security one-pager.

[17:00] Jasmine: A few product-y Qs: can we do tool-chains — e.g., retrieval -> model -> tool-call -> rerank across languages?
[17:10] Priya: Yes. Redwood supports chained tool-calling flows. You can have the runtime orchestrate retrieval, pass chunks into the model, call external APIs, and then run a reranker model as a final step. This is how we recommend avoiding hallucination: keep authoritative data sources as tools rather than free-text only.

[19:05] Lena: Are there known gaps with certain OSS models on math/facts? We've seen strange numeracy issues with some quantized builds.
[19:14] Priya: Numeracy can regress with heavy quantization and with models not fine-tuned for instruction. For critical numeric tasks we recommend smaller targeted evals and, if needed, a larger non-quantized model in the critical path. Redwood Optimize can surface these tradeoffs per prompt set.

[21:00] Evan: Competitors— have you already evaluated CloudAI or ModelCorp?
[21:05] Lena: We've trialed CloudAI's managed endpoints, and looked at ModelCorp self-host; both had limits on long context or required expensive premium tiers. Their tool-calling felt less mature than what you described.

[22:10] Priya: Understood. We'll show a benchmark that highlights context window throughput and tail latencies.

[25:00] Deep technical exchange (SE and Infra) — transcript becomes more granular and technical, some crosstalk and mis-transcriptions:
[25:08] Marcus: For the dedicated pool, what's the recommended instance types? We prefer H100 for throughput but cost is big.
[25:18] Priya: H100 or next gen equivalence for 65k windows on 70B class. For cost-sensitive 32k you can use A100-80GB with kernel-level optimizations. Also mention of 'KV cache sharding' — this reduces per-request memory in multi-tenant scenarios.
[26:30] Marcus: Do you support mixed-precision and dynamic kernel selection?
[26:36] Priya: Yes. The runtime picks kernels based on model arch, sequence length, and observed distribution. We also do continuous batching; you can tune batch latency tradeoff.

[28:10] Lena: A small worry — tool-calling security. If model suggests executing a DB command, we want strict allow-listing.
[28:20] Priya: Absolutely. Redwood's function signatures are allow-listed; you control which functions the model can call. We also support a policy layer to block or require approvals for dangerous operations.

[30:00] Jasmine: On multilingual evaluation — will Redwood help set up tests?
[30:06] Priya: Yes we have templates for multilingual eval sets and can help run them and generate side-by-side metrics (BLEU-ish, factuality scores, hallucination counts).

[33:00] Discussion about measuring hallucination and guardrails; brief side-track where a proprietary model name is mis-heard:
[33:10] Marcus: We read some papers on "LumaX" that looked promising — is that a Redwood verified model?
[33:18] Priya: I think you mean LlamaX or Luma — there's a lot of forks and naming is messy. We'll propose a vetted list; Redwood-verified models have performance profiles and safety evaluations.

[36:00] Evan: Ok to recap: customer wants to pilot hosted + dedicated comparisons focusing on 65k retrieval/ reasoning, tool-calling determinism and Spanish/Chinese quality. Redwood will prepare pricing, security docs, and a pilot proposal.

[36:25] Lena: Yes, and we want to see concrete numbers on tail latencies for worst-case queries. Also a plan for scaling at month-end spikes.

[38:40] Priya: For spikes we can configure autoscaling and burst to a shared pool, or reserve extra capacity during month end. We'll include recommended autoscale policy examples.

[40:05] Evan: Anything else on procurement or legal hoops?
[40:12] Marcus: We'll need a standard DPA and to confirm we can do a data processing addendum with specific retention clauses. Also vendor assessment may request pen-test evidence.

[41:00] Evan: We'll route legal to supply DPA and SOC2 docs. For pen-test we can provide previous reports and coordinate a new one if required for private deployments.

[44:00] Jasmine: Can we get an initial demo of function-calling today or is that part of the SE bench later?
[44:06] Priya: We can give a short live example now — show a tool function call flow and a retrieval->call->rerank mini-demo. Quick share screen demo happens (not in transcript) — showed a function signature being defined and a sample call.

[47:30] Lena: That demo helped. I'm more confident about the function API. Couple of follow-ups: can we lock down the function outputs schema and force model to return structured JSON?
[47:40] Priya: Yes, you can define strict output schemas. The runtime will validate and reject non-conforming responses.

[49:00] Final recap and next steps:
[49:05] Evan: Action items — I will send pricing + security one-pager. Priya will prepare demo scripts and a bench plan. Lena will share sanitized prompts and sample docs. We'll book a 60-min benchmark (SE + Marcus) next week.
[49:25] Lena: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[49:30] Marcus: Thanks.
[49:32] Jasmine: Appreciate it.

[51:00] End recording.
